questions.q: What is the term for the 'passive cooling' technique that uses the buoyancy of heated air to exhaust hot air through high-level openings?
questions.n: Also known as the chimney effect, it relies on the principle that warm air is less dense and rises, creating a natural pressure difference.

questions.q: Which building orientation is most ideal in the Philippines to minimize direct solar heat gain on the long sides of the building?
questions.n: By aligning the long axis East-West, the major facades face North and South, where solar heat gain is easier to control with simple overhangs.

questions.q: What is the name of the external sun-shading device that consists of horizontal or vertical slats to block direct sunlight while allowing air to pass through?
questions.n: This French term translates to 'sun-breaker' and is a staple of tropical modernism popularized by architects like Le Corbusier.

questions.q: To encourage 'Cross Ventilation,' where should the outlet openings be placed in relation to the inlet openings?
o: Directly opposite or diagonal to the inlet
At a higher elevation than the inlet only
questions.n: This placement forces the air to travel across the entire space, effectively removing stagnant heat and humidity.

questions.q: What is the term for the 'secondary roof' or a ventilated attic space that acts as a thermal buffer between the sun-heated roof and the living space?
questions.n: This ventilated cavity prevents the direct transfer of solar heat from the roofing material to the ceiling below.

questions.q: What is the term for the strategy of using 'thermal mass' (like thick concrete or stone) to absorb heat during the day and release it at night?
questions.n: Thermal mass acts as a 'heat battery,' soaking up energy when the sun is out and radiating it back when temperatures drop.

questions.q: What is Xeriscaping, often used in sustainable landscape architecture?
o: A method of planting only underwater species.
A landscaping method using drought-tolerant plants to minimize irrigation.
The use of plastic plants to save on maintenance.
questions.n: By selecting plants adapted to dry conditions, the landscape requires little to no supplemental water.

questions.q: Which sustainable strategy involves collecting, filtering, and storing water from the roof for non-potable uses?
questions.n: Capturing precipitation reduces the demand on municipal water supplies and mitigates stormwater runoff issues.

questions.q: What is the difference between 'Greywater' and 'Blackwater'?
o: Greywater comes from sinks/showers; Blackwater comes from toilets.
There is no difference; both must be sent to the sewer.
Greywater is clean tap water; Blackwater is rainwater.
Greywater is industrial waste; Blackwater is residential waste.
questions.n: Greywater lacks fecal contamination and is easier to treat for reuse, whereas blackwater contains pathogens and sewage.

questions.q: What is the name of the 'living' roof system that is partially or completely covered with vegetation to provide insulation?
questions.n: Also known as an eco-roof, it reduces the urban heat island effect and improves the building's thermal performance.

questions.q: Which brick bond consists of alternating courses of 'Stretchers' (the long side) and 'Headers' (the short side)?
questions.n: This bond is exceptionally strong because one entire row of headers locks into the row of stretchers above and below.

questions.q: What bond features each course consisting of alternating Stretchers and Headers?
questions.n: This creates a distinctive checkered pattern that is highly prized for its aesthetic appearance.

questions.q: Which bond is composed entirely of 'Stretchers' and is commonly used for thin cavity walls?
questions.n: Also called a running bond, it is the most common pattern for modern half-brick thick walls.

questions.q: What is a 'Soldier' course in brickwork?
o: Bricks laid flat with the short end showing.
A brick that has been cut in half.
Bricks laid horizontally on their narrow side.
Bricks laid vertically on their ends with the narrow face showing.
questions.n: Often used for lintels or decorative bands, soldiers 'stand' tall like their namesake.

questions.q: Which bond is similar to the English bond but has the stretchers shifted by half a brick in every other stretcher course, creating a 'stepped' appearance?
questions.n: By offsetting the vertical joints in the stretcher courses, it creates a unique diagonal pattern on the wall face.

questions.q: What is the most common structural challenge when converting an old warehouse into a modern office or residential space?
questions.n: Warehouses were built for storage, but modern occupancy codes for offices often require higher load-bearing capacities for safety.

questions.q: In the context of the National Building Code, what is the difficulty in repurposing heritage homes into commercial spaces?
o: The building is too old to be painted.
Compliance with Modern Fire Safety and Accessibility (BP 344).
questions.n: Integrating ramps, elevators, and fire exits without destroying historic fabric is a major regulatory and design conflict.

questions.q: What do you call the chemical or physical deterioration of building materials over time that must be addressed before reuse?
questions.n: Rusting rebar, rotting timber, and crumbling masonry are all forms of degradation that compromise building integrity.

questions.q: Why is 'Hazardous Material Abatement' a frequent challenge in adaptive reuse projects from the mid-20th century?
o: The concrete is too hard to drill.
The presence of asbestos or lead-based paint.
questions.n: These materials were common in the past but are now known to be toxic and require specialized, expensive removal.

questions.q: What is the term for the 'conflict' that arises when an old building’s layout is too rigid to accommodate modern MEP systems?
questions.n: Thick walls and low ceilings in historic buildings often leave no room for modern HVAC ducts or electrical conduits.

questions.q: In the Philippines, what is the 'Habagat' and how does it affect tropical design?
o: A type of indigenous roofing material made of palm leaves.
The term for a traditional Filipino courtyard.
The Northeast Monsoon that brings cool breezes.
The Southwest Monsoon, bringing heavy rain and wind from June to September.
questions.n: Architects must design building envelopes to be watertight and structurally sound against these seasonal wind-driven rains.

questions.q: What is the primary function of a 'Light Well' in a sustainable multi-story building?
o: To house the building's elevator cables.
To act as a garbage chute.
To bring natural daylight and ventilation to the deeper parts of a building floor plate.
questions.n: This reduces the reliance on artificial lighting and mechanical cooling in the core of the building.

questions.q: In brickwork, what is a 'Header'?
o: The long face of a brick laid horizontally.
A brick laid at a 45-degree angle.
The short square end of a brick showing on the face of a wall.
The person in charge of the masonry crew.
questions.n: Headers are used to tie different layers of a brick wall together structurally.

questions.q: What is 'Façadism' in the context of adaptive reuse?
o: Painting a mural on the side of a building.
Designing a building with no windows on the front.
The study of different types of building faces.
Preserving only the exterior shell or facade of a historic building while constructing a new interior.
questions.n: It is a controversial practice that keeps the visual history while allowing for a completely modern use inside.

questions.q: What is a 'Thermal Bridge' and why is it problematic in sustainable design?
o: A fireplace designed to look like a bridge.
A path of least resistance for heat to bypass a building's insulation.
A walkway connecting two heated buildings.
A specialized tool used to measure heat.
questions.n: Highly conductive materials like steel or aluminum can 'leak' heat through walls, reducing energy efficiency.
